newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council disappointed at delay over W. Sahara.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council disappointed at delay over W. Sahara.

text.p: The Security Council expressed disappointment on Wednesday at the lack of progress in organising a referendum to decide whether Western Sahara should be incorporated into Morocco or become independent.

A statement read at a brief council meeting prompted by a recent report by Secretary-General Kofi Annan concurred with his assessment that it was essential to maintain the ceasefire in force in the former Spanish territory since September 1991. It said any breach "could seriously threaten regional stability."
"The Security Council ... is disappointed at the lack of progress on the implementation of the plan for the settlement of the question of Western Sahara noted in the report," it said.

The ceasefire halted fighting between Morocco and guerrillas of the Polisario Front, which seeks independence. But the referendum, originally set for January 1992, has been repeatedly postponed due to disagreement over who should be allowed to vote.

The Security Council said the presence of a force called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), now reduced to some 230 military observers and support personnel, had been "essential in helping the parties to maintain their commitment to the ceasefire."

The council expressed strong support for Annan's efforts to overcome the stalemate and welcomed his appointment this week of a personal envoy for the region -- former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker. It urged the parties to cooperate with him fully.

Baker is expected to hold talks next month with the Moroccan government, the leadership of Polisario and the governments of Algeria and Mauritania, neighbouring countries closely involved in the issue. Polisario's main base is at Tindouf, on the Algerian side of the border with Western Sahara.

Baker will see whether the U.N. plan can be implemented in its present form, whether adjustments acceptable to the two sides might be possible or whether other ways of resolving the conflict could be found.
